newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Experts, crew tackle Russian space collision.
newsitem.headline: Experts, crew tackle Russian space collision.

text.p: Experts and the crew of the Russian space station Mir face a tough task minimising the damage from its collision with a cargo craft, an incident which had raised new doubts about the safety of Moscow's space programme.
The unmanned Progress cargo craft collided on Wednesday with the Spektr scientific module attached to the main section of Mir, causing a partial loss of air pressure.

Russian space officials described the collision as "the most serious accident in recent times" involving the vessel but said there was no immediate danger to the U.S. astronaut Michael Foale and Russians Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin.

Despite the comparative safety of Foale, the chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives Science Committee urged NASA on Wednesday to begin a safety review of the Mir before any more U.S. astronauts went on board for a long-term stay.

The head of the Russian mission control, Vladimir Lobachyov, told a news conference on Wednesday that the Progress had punctured the scientific module and may have damaged one of the solar batteries, creating energy problems.

"The cosmonauts say there is a fall in the electrical supply...and as a result of the collision a hole (in the scientific module used for the docking) has developed whose size is still unclear," he said.
A spokesman for the U.S. space agency NASA said on Wednesday that the crew had been able to seal off the damaged compartment.

Russian officials said the crew had sufficient water and food on board. But Vladimir Solovyov, responsible for flight coordination, conceded that an eighth of the Mir station was temporarily out of action because of the collision.
Lobachyov said a special commission comprising officials and experts had been set up to consider the situation and work out recommendations.

Interfax news agency quoted Russian officials as saying a space walk by the cosmonauts might be needed to get the details of what had happened and estimate the damage. They did not say when the space walk might take place.
The launch of the next cargo craft, set for June 27, will probably be postponed, Lobachyov said.
He said a commission would decide Spektr's fate and it might be undocked from the space station. Lobachyov said the Progress was expected to fall to Earth and sink into the Pacific Ocean on Friday.
NASA officials said the Mir crew could leave at any time in a three-seat Russian Soyuz spacecraft but the evacuation of the station was not planned.

James Sensenbrenner, the chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives Science Committee, asked NASA to comply voluntarily with legislation that would bar U.S. astronauts from going on board Mir for a long-term stay until the safety tests are passed.

The House recently passed a bill, the Civilian Space Authorisation, containing a rule that no U.S. astronaut be placed on board Mir for a long-term stay until the National Aeronatics and Space Administration certifies to Congress that the space station meets or exceeds U.S. safety standards. It is not yet law.

Mir, the world's only space station, was launched in 1986 and has suffered a series of malfunctions in recent months, including a fire and a leakage of coolant. It is due to be replaced by an international station in the next few years.
